text: Our Moon is slowly breaking up with us. Mars has the opposite problem.
Its moon, Phobos, is clingy. It orbits just six thousand kilometres above the ground. Our Moon keeps sixty times more space.
sub: Its moon, Phobos, is clingy. It orbits just 6,000 km above the ground. Our Moon keeps 60 times more space.

text: It's so close, it laps Mars three times a day. From the ground, it rises in the west, and sets in the east.
sub: It's so close, it laps Mars 3 times a day. From the ground, it rises in the west, and sets in the east.

text: And it's moving in. About two metres closer, every century.
sub: And it's moving in. About 2 metres closer, every century.

text: Same physics as our Moon, just backwards. Phobos circles faster than Mars spins, so the tidal bulge it raises lags behind it, and drags it down.
Mars is basically pulling it in for a hug it won't survive.
You can already see the strain. Those long grooves? Scientists think they may be stretch marks, from Mars pulling on it.
NASA's Perseverance rover even filmed it crossing the Sun. The eclipse lasted just over forty seconds.
sub: NASA's Perseverance rover even filmed it crossing the Sun. The eclipse lasted just over 40 seconds.

text: In thirty to fifty million years, Mars will tear it apart, and the pieces could spread into a ring.
sub: In 30 to 50 million years, Mars will tear it apart, and the pieces could spread into a ring.

text: So Mars finally puts a ring on it.
Meanwhile, its other moon, Deimos, is quietly drifting away. Just like ours.
And their names? Phobos and Deimos. Fear, and Dread. Red planet. Red flags.
So which would you rather have? A moon that leaves you, or one that never lets go?
